By Wojciech Moskwa, Bloomberg News The proposed permanent U.S. military base in Poland, dubbed Fort Trump, will cost as much as 17 billion zloty ($4.4 billion) and could open as early as in 2029, according to a report from newspaper Rzeczpospolita. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said in New York this week that Poland, a NATO member and a front-line state to Russia’s war on Ukraine, is nearing a deal with the U.S. on deploying a permanent presence of U.S. troops. President Karol Nawrocki told Bloomberg TV that if the two nations finalize the deal, the compound would be called Fort Trump. Poland’s National Security Bureau said talks with the U.S. administration include a permanently stationed base of about 5,000 soldiers, according to Rzeczpospolita. Earlier, Sikorski said the planned military installation could host about 10,000 troops, compared with about 7,000 rotational U.S. soldiers currently stationed in Poland. The negotiations come amid broader European concerns that Washington may reduce its military presence on the continent. President Donald Trump has told European allies they need to take greater responsibility for their own security, while Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is conducting a review of U.S. forces deployed on the other side of the Atlantic. The exact location of the permanent base will depend on what type of U.S. troops are stationed in Poland, Rzeczpospolita reported. Sites near Wroclaw, Poznan and Szczecin — all cities in western Poland closer to Germany than they are Ukraine — are under consideration, it added. ©2026 Bloomberg L.P. Visit bloomberg.com. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/21/new-.text: Romania on Tuesday swore in a new cabinet following a vote that ended a months-long political impasse.Prime Minister Luca Niculescu, an independent diplomat, won 280 votes in favour of his proposed cabinet, with 58 against. He plans to start work immediately, with a large budget deficit at the top of his agenda.President Nicușor Dan nominated Niculescu, 55, a diplomat and former journalist, on 5 October, the president’s fourth pick for the job, after three earlier nominees failed to form a government.Niculescu was widely expected to succeed after securing pledges of support for a minority government from the Social Democrats and other parties. He has reportedly reached a deal with several parties for six months of backing while a longer-term agreement is negotiated.Speaking in Parliament after the vote, he thanked lawmakers for trusting his cabinet.“I present a governing programme, a team, and a commitment to work toward several clear objectives,” he said. “And I want to tell the Romanian people, from the very start, what kind of government this will be. A government that brings funds and investments into the country.”The political crisis gripped Romania since MayThe political crisis has gripped Romania since May, when then-Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan was ousted in a no-confidence motion. The motion was filed jointly by the Social Democratic Party, which had been part of his governing coalition, and the Alliance for the Unity of Romanians party. Bolojan’s government had pursued strict austerity measures.Bolojan took office in 2025 with the aim of ending one of Romania’s worst political crises since the end of communism and of reducing a massive budget deficit.Romania has faced a long stretch of instability since the annulment of a presidential election in December 2024. The country has also struggled with rampant inflation and a technical recession. Last year, it recorded one of the highest budget deficits in the European Union.Tuesday’s vote came weeks after lawmakers rejected a cabinet proposed by Dan’s third pick, Siegfried Muresan. That failure prolonged the crisis and raised the prospect of early elections, at a time of regional security concerns linked to Russia’s war in neighbouring Ukraine. Romania is a member of both NATO and the EU.Experts warn that tensions could flare again soon. Niculescu’s support rests on a six-month arrangement with several parties, and a longer-term deal has yet to be agreed.
